reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Middleton's Allergy
clinicalPearls: Serum sickness is the classic immune-complex (type III) hypersensitivity reaction, presenting with fever, rash, arthralgia or arthritis, and lymphadenopathy
Symptoms characteristically begin about one to three weeks after first exposure to the offending agent, with a faster onset on re-exposure because the patient is already sensitised
Historically it followed heterologous (animal) antiserum, and today it is most often triggered by antitoxins, antivenoms, therapeutic antibodies, and certain drugs
The rash is often urticarial or a serpiginous purplish eruption at the border of the palms and soles, a helpful clinical clue
During the active phase complement is consumed, so serum C3 and C4 fall and can be used to support the diagnosis and track resolution

A serum-sickness-like reaction, most often attributed to antibiotics such as cefaclor, resembles serum sickness clinically but lacks the true immune-complex and hypocomplementaemic features and is generally benign
The condition is usually self-limiting once the causative agent is withdrawn, with recovery over days to a couple of weeks
Management principles are stopping and avoiding the trigger, symptomatic relief with antihistamines and anti-inflammatory agents, and corticosteroids for severe or systemic disease
reference.pathophysiology: Serum sickness is mediated by circulating antigen-antibody (immune) complexes. After exposure to a foreign protein or drug-protein conjugate, the host mounts an antibody response; as antibody rises while antigen is still present, soluble immune complexes form in antigen-relative excess. These complexes deposit in small vessels of the skin, joints, kidneys, and elsewhere, where they activate complement and recruit neutrophils, producing local inflammation and tissue injury (a type III hypersensitivity reaction). Complement activation consumes C3 and C4, accounting for the transient hypocomplementaemia. Once the antigen is cleared and complexes are removed, the process resolves. Serum-sickness-like reactions produce a similar clinical picture through incompletely understood mechanisms without demonstrable immune-complex disease.
additionalDifferentials: Acute viral infection (e.g. hepatitis B, parvovirus) with rash and arthralgia
Systemic lupus erythematosus and other connective-tissue disease
Urticarial vasculitis and other small-vessel vasculitides
Acute drug reaction such as DRESS or an urticarial drug eruption
additionalInvestigations: Serum C3 and C4, which fall during the active immune-complex phase
Full blood count and inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP)
Assessment for circulating immune complexes or cryoglobulins where available
Serologies to exclude viral and autoimmune mimics
Skin biopsy in atypical cases to evaluate for vasculitis
redFlags: Significant renal involvement with proteinuria, haematuria, or rising creatinine
Concurrent anaphylaxis or angioedema at the time of re-exposure to the antigen
Neurologic involvement or severe systemic illness suggesting extensive immune-complex disease
Features pointing to a severe drug reaction such as DRESS rather than simple serum sickness
reference.prognosis: Serum sickness is generally self-limiting and resolves without sequelae once the causative agent is removed, with symptoms settling over days to a couple of weeks. Recovery may be hastened by corticosteroids in severe cases; significant organ involvement is uncommon but warrants closer follow-up.
pitfalls: Failing to take a careful exposure history for antisera, antivenoms, or therapeutic antibodies given weeks earlier
Confusing serum sickness with an acute IgE-mediated allergic reaction and mismanaging the tempo of illness
Overlooking renal involvement by not checking urinalysis and renal function
Re-administering the same heterologous protein or drug without recognising the sensitisation risk
